What should be mandatory in high school curriculum?
I agree if you mean in general and not focusing on one belief system.
I assume that's what /u/Arotaes_Forgehammer meant. I think it would be great to have it taught in conjunction with Philosophy though, because that also helps, especially in critical thinking.

It's said often and I tend to agree with the idea. A finance/tax-type course would go a long way in explaining things like interest, tax, and general principles that folks will need as they enter society on their own.
In addition to what is generally offered now I'd argue for courses in critical thinking skills, basic credit/financial management, and some serious goddamn physical fitness emphasis.

Critical thinking is the first thing they try to engrain in your head in college (at least in a couple of my courses eg. English 101). There is absolutely no reason we should wait until college to start teaching kids to think for themselves.

I think something akin to a college course I once took. It was called "Marriage and Family" but really focused on relationship dynamics. I didn't take until I was 23 and was baffled at how much it could have helped.

Look at all these redflags my previous partners have. Look at how much I let friends and family walk all over me. Learning to fight fairly. Learning to communicate with a loved one before you're yelling at each other and throwing all those things you've been bottling up as weapons.
Everyone should be able to use basic hand tools, change a tire, snake a drain, and skin a cat.

Physical education.

Done right, not the trial of passage it currently is. We could raise the first healthiest generation of kid that the world had ever seen. Rather than a generation riddled with diabetes and obesity. Proper physical education would also probably have a huge psychological benefit, reducing depression and disaffection in out teens.
P.E. paired with a health class would be great. Alternating schedule, some days you exercise, some days you learn about nutrition, sex and the safety precautions, and how to live a healthy lifestyle.

Logic. Stuff like basic discreet math, and possibly a very basic circuits class.

This would encourage logical reasoning and help those that aren't chasing a college degree succeed in physical labor work. Having some logical thinking can go a long way.
A class solely focused on public speaking.
Basic cooking skills. Eating is essential to survival. Being able to cook for yourself can also potentially help with the obesity issue. Less premade processed foods, more nutritious whole foods.

Real arts classes. Not some frilly school choir or basic painting, but something much more rigorous, like a music theory class or art history course. Most other fields are very similar to the arts, and the mental flexibility to apply certain skills in an artistic form could be extremely beneficial in the long run.

Conservatism.

I firmly believe that most people, when exposed to true conservatism, lean that direction.

This seems kinda like a bad idea.....exposing kids to multiple different ideals is much better, and allows them to choose one that they believe in. My high school history teacher tried to give reasons and ideals behind a certain political belief, which really changed my view on certain things. One specific example was the Nazis...although he agreed most of the things they did were absolutely terrible and unthinkable, he also saw how they could become such fanatics through Volkism ( if you want a link: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%B6lkisch_movement). The opportunity to see the world in a different perspective helped me much more than the ranting on about liberal or conservative politics. (As a side note, I really like how you didn't get downvoted into the ground like you would on reddit for bringing up conservatism....that community immediately attacked all non-liberal ideals on reddit.)

I think our choices for a life after graduation should be more clear. I was always told you go to college for four years or you're paid minimum wage for the rest of your life. Now that I'm looking at 40k debt at the end of my four years, I'm realizing I could have had gone so many less expensive routes.

How to budget your money (That should also be manditory for anyone on Welfare)

Comparative religion, to help foster critical thinking skills and expose young people who might have been insulated in one faith to other belief systems. I'm an atheist, but I think it's important for everyone to be aware of religious belief systems because they tend to affect law and culture.

Harm Reduction form of drug education, but that should start before highschool.

I'd say comprehensive sex ed (including forms of birth control other than abstinence, as well as LGBT stuff, and using words like "when the penis goes in the vagina" instead of "when the man goes inside the woman") but kids should be learning about condoms and abortions in middle school and I even support age appropriate sex ed in younger grades.

I would like to see a class taught to show the students their full rights and how to interact with the law. I don't believe the majority of people understand their full rights that they have when interacting with police.
How to do your fucking taxes, took me years to learn and I still have to get it checked

Basic automotive maintenance. I have seen so many younger people that have no idea on how to check their oil/tire pressure, how to change a flat tire or a burnt out bulb. It is so very basic yet it alludes so many younger people.

First Aid course! It would be so easy to implement, just put in a health class. Basic first aid is an essential skill that everyone should have the opportunity to learn. A few weeks of curriculum and you can also give them a level 1 first aid certificate which they can add to their resumes. You never know when you might need you training, and when it happens they'll have the confidence they need to provide help.
Course involving a trade. Learn how to plumbing, carpentry, nursing, welding, blacksmith, IT network administrator or anything that involves using your hands.

Personal Finance and Micro Economics, Practical Civics, Basic Home and Auto Maintenance, Nutrition, Health and Fitness (this would include SexEd), Mathematics, Language, Culture (Music, Art, History and Philosophy) and Science (Intro/Physics/Chem/Bio- in that order with electives in Astronomy, Advanced Physics and Ecology).
Teach kids how to cope. A lot of people don't really know how to cope when they're faced with difficulties. Most of the times end up hurting themselves or people around them.

Because of the obesity issue, I propose a mandatory fitness test to graduate high school.

At least 25 feet up on a rock wall.

At the very minimum 10 pull-ups in 5 minutes

No less than 100 crunches in 2 minutes

Oh, and a 5 mile run in no more than 35 minutes.

When you are in the kind of shape it would require to perform this, you won't stop most likely.

Also, this cannot be waived if you fail or have an an IEP. (My older brothers got one) if you cannot maintain yourself you don't need the opportunity to be in the workforce. Fuck, from what I know even McDonald's requires a high school diploma.

Budgeting, Laundry, and Basic cooking.

Basically there should be a "How to live alone and not suck at life" course.

Programming and basic computer knowledge. You can't let high school students go into a world based on technology without some basic knowledge of tech. Programming is so valuable in today's world that students should at least learn a small amount in a math class or a dedicated programming class. Programming also could help teach certain math sections, as it is very logical (most of the time).

Doesn't matter what you put in the curriculum, you cannot force people to learn anything. One example, in a country whose only language is English, so many people cannot conjugate a verb or show possession correctly, or figure out how to use an apostrophe correctly.
Home ec and budgeting. It's all well and good to know how to calculate the square root of the area of an isosceles triangle or whatever, but some things are more important than that.
